'''whimbrel''' (hwim′brel), ''n.'' [Also ''wimbrel''; perhaps for *''whimmerel'', so called with ref. to its peculiar cry, < ''whimmer'' + ''-el''.] The jack-curlew or half-curlew of Europe, ''Numenius phæopus'', smaller than the curlew proper, ''N. arquatus'', and very closely related to the Hudsonian curlew of North America, ''N. hudsonicus''. Also called ''tang-whaup'', ''May whaup'', and ''little whaup'' (which see, under ''whaup'').

'''whim-gin''' (hwim′jin), ''n.'' [< ''whim''<sup>1</sup> + ''gin''<sup>4</sup>.] Same as ''whim''<sup>1</sup>, 3.

'''whimling†''' (hwim′ling), ''n.'' [Also corruptly ''whimlen''; < ''whim''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.] A person full of whims.

{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Coxcomb, iv. 7.}}}}

'''whimmer''' (hwim′ėr), ''v. i.'' [Var. of ''whimper''; cf. G. ''wimmern'', moan.] Same as ''whimper''. [Scotch.]

'''whimmy''' (hwim′i), ''a.'' [< ''whim''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Full of whims; whimsical.

¶
'''whimper''' (hwim′pėr), ''v.'' [Also (Sc.) ''whimmer''; = LG. ''wemeren'' = G. ''wimmern'', whimper; cf. MHG. ''wimmer'', n., whining; ''gewammer'', whining; perhaps ult. connected with ''whine''.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To cry with a low, whining, broken voice; make a low, complaining sound.
{{smaller block|<poem>Speak, ''whimp’ring'' Younglings, and make known
The reason why
Ye droop and weep.</poem>
{{right|''Herrick'', To Primroses fill’d with Morning Dew.}}
The little brook that ''whimpered'' by his school-house.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 424.}}}}
'''2.''' To tell tales. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To utter in a low, whining, or crying tone.
{{smaller block|<poem>Poverty with most who ''whimper'' forth
Their long complaints, is self-inflicted woe.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 429.}}}}

'''whimper''' (hwim′pėr), ''n.'' [< ''whimper'', ''v.'' Cf. MHG. ''wimmer'', whimper, crying, whining.] A low, peevish, broken cry; a whine.
{{smaller block|<poem>The loved caresses of the maid
The dogs with crouch and ''whimper'' paid.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., ii. 24.}}}}

'''To be on the whimper''', to be in a peevish, crying state. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Mrs. Mountain ''is'' constantly ''on the whimper'' when George’s name is mentioned. ''Thackeray'', Virginians, xii.}}

'''whimperer''' (hwim′pėr-ėr), ''n.'' [< ''whimper'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who whimpers.
{{smaller block|No effeminate knight, no ''whimperer'', like his brother.
{{right|''Jarvis'', tr. of Don Quixote, i. 1.}}}}

{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 429.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>The loved caresses of the maid
The dogs with crouch and ''whimper'' paid.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., ii. 24.}}}}

{{smaller block|No effeminate knight, no ''whimperer'', like his brother.
{{right|''Jarvis'', tr. of Don Quixote, i. 1.}}}}

'''whimpering''' (hwim′pėr-ing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''whimper, v.'']   A low, whining cry; a whimper.
{{smaller block|Liue in puling and ''whimpering'' & heuines of hert.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 90.}}}}
{{smaller block|He will not be put off with solemn ''whimperings'', hypocritical confessions, rueful faces.
{{right|''Dr. H. More'', Mystery of Godliness (1660), p. 509. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''whimperingly''' (hwim′pėr-ing-li), ''adv.'' In a whimpering or whining manner.
{{smaller block|“’T was n’t my fault!” he ''whimperingly'' declared.
{{right|''St. Nicholas'', XVIII. 176.}}}}

'''whimple''' (hwim′pl), ''n.'' and ''v.'' An erroneous form of ''wimple''.

'''whimsey''', ''n.'', ''a.'' and ''v.'' See ''whimsy''.

'''whimsey-shaft''' (hwim′zi-shȧft), ''n.'' Same as ''whim-shaft''.

'''whim-shaft''' (hwim′shȧft), ''n.'' In ''mining'', a shaft at which there is a whim for hoisting the ore.
{{smaller block|In shallow mines and in regions where fuel is very scarce (as in Mexico) most of the hoisting is done by horse-power and the use of the whim: called in Derbyshire, England, where this mode of raising the ore was formerly almost exclusively used, a ''horse-engine shaft''. See cut under ''whim''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''whimsical''' (hwim′zi-kal), ''a.''   [< ''whims(y)'' + ''-ic'' + ''-al''.]   '''1.''' Full of whims; freakish; having odd fancies or peculiar notions; capricious.
{{smaller block|There is another circumstance in which I am particular, or, as my neighbors call me, ''whimsical'': as my garden invites into it all the birds, . . . I do not suffer any one to destroy their nests.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 477.}}}}
{{smaller block|How humoursome, how ''whimsical'' soever we may appear, there’s one fixed principle that runs through almost the whole race of us.
{{right|''Vanbrugh'', Æsop, V. i.}}}} '''2.''' Odd; fantastic.
{{smaller block|In one of the chambers is a ''whimsical'' chayre, which folded into so many varieties as to turn into a bed, a bolster, a table, or a couch.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Nov. 29, 1644.}}}}
{{smaller block|The . . . gentry now dispersed, the ''whimsical'' misfortune which had befallen the gens d’armerie of Tillietudlem furnishing them with huge entertainment on their road homeward.
{{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, iii.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' ''Singular'', ''Odd'', etc. (see ''eccentric''), notional, crotchety.—'''2.''' Fanciful, grotesque.}}

'''whimsicality''' (hwim-zi-kal′i-ti), ''n.''   [< ''whimsical'' + ''-ity''.]   '''1.''' The state or character of being whimsical; whimsicalness.
{{smaller block|The ''whimsicality'' of my father’s brain was so far from having the whole honor of this as it had of almost all his other strange notions.
{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, iii. 33.}}}}
'''2.''' Oddity; strangeness; fantasticalness.
{{smaller block|It was a new position for Mr. Lyon to find his prospective rank seemingly an obstacle to anything he desired. For a moment the ''whimsicality'' of it interrupted the current of his feeling.
{{right|''C. D. Warner'', Little Journey in the World, v.}}}}
'''3.''' Pl. ''whimsicalities'' (-tiz). That which exhibits whimsical or fanciful qualities; a whimsical thought, saying, or action.
{{smaller block|To pass from these sparkling ''whimsicalities'' to the almost Quaker-like gravity, decorum, and restraint of the essay “On the Life and Writings of Mr. Isaac Disraeli” is an almost bewildering transition.
{{right|''The Academy'', April 25, 1891, p. 389.}}}}

'''whimsically''' (hwim′zi-kal-i), ''adv.'' In a whimsical manner; freakishly.
{{smaller block|There is not . . . a more ''whimsically'' dismal figure in nature than a man of real modesty who assumes an air of impudence.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', The Bee, No. 1.}}}}

'''whimsicalness''' (hwim′zi-kal-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being whimsical; whimsicality; freakishness; whimsical disposition; odd temper. ''Pope'', Letter to Miss Blount.

'''whimsy, whimsey''' (hwim′zi), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [Appar. from an unrecorded verb ''whimse'', be unsteady, < Norw. ''kvimsa'', skip, whisk, jump from one thing to another, = Sw. dial. ''hvimsa'', be unsteady, giddy, or dizzy, = Dan. ''vimse'', skip, jump, etc.: see ''whim''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''n.''; pl. ''whimsies'', ''whimseys'' (-ziz). '''1.''' A whim; a freak; a capricious notion.
{{smaller block|I cannot but smile at this man’s preposterous ''whimsies''.
{{right|''Milton'', Ans. to Salmasius, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I court others in Verse, but I love thee in Prose;
And they have my ''Whimsies'', but thou hast my Heart.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Better Answer to Cloe Jealous, st. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Wearing out life in his religious whim
Till his religious ''whimsey'' wears out him.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Truth, l. 90.}}}}
'''2.''' Same as ''whim''<sup>1</sup>, 3; also, a small warehouse-crane for lifting goods to the upper stories. ''E. H. Knight.''—'''3.''' See the quotation.
{{smaller block|The table [of crown-glass], as it is now called, is carried off, laid flat upon a support called a ''whimsey''.
{{right|''Glass-making'', p. 124.}}}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Full of whims or fancies; whimsical; changeable.
{{smaller block|Jeer on, my ''whimsy'' lady.
{{right|''Shirley'', Hyde Park, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet reveries are fleeting things,
That come and go on ''whimsy'' wings.</poem>
{{right|''F. Locker'', Arcadia.}}}}

'''whimsy†, whimsey†''' (hwim′zi), ''v. t.''   [< ''whimsy'', ''n.'']   To fill with whimsies.
<poem>Jewels, and plate, and fooleries molest me;
To have a man’s brains ''whimsied'' with his wealth!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'', Rule a Wife, ii. 2.}}}}

'''whimsy-board†''' (hwim′zi-bōrd), ''n.'' A board or tray on which different objects were carried about for sale.
{{smaller block|I am sometimes a small retainer to a billiard-table, and sometimes, when the master of it is sick, earn a penny by a ''whimsy-board.'' {{right|''Tom Brown'', Works, II. 17. (''Davies.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Then pippins did in wheel-barrows abound,
And oranges in ''whimsey-boards'' went round;
Bess Hoy first found it troublesome to bawl,
And therefore plac’d her cherries on a stall.</poem>
{{right|''W. King'', Art of Cookery, l. 342.}}}}

'''whimwham''' (hwim′hwam), ''n.''   [A varied reduplication of ''whim''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''flimflam.'']   A plaything; a toy; a freak or whim; an odd device.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nay, not that way;
They’ll pull you all to pieces for your ''whim-whams'',
Your garters, and your gloves.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher and Shirley'', Night-Walker, i. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Your studied ''whim-whams'', and your fine set faces—
What have these got ye? proud and harsh opinions.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, iii. 1.}}}}

'''whin<sup>1</sup>''' (hwin), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''whynne''; < ME. ''whynne'', ''quyn'', gorse, furze, < W. ''chwyn'', weeds, a weed; cf. Bret. ''chouenna'', weed.]   '''1.''' A plant of the genus ''Ulex'', the furze or gorse, chiefly ''U. Europæus'' and ''U. nanus''. See ''furze'', 1, and cut under ''Ulex''.
{{smaller block|With thornes, breres, and moni a ''quyn''.
{{right|''Ywain and Gawain'', l. 150. (''Skeat.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whynnes'' or hethe—bruiere. {{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 288.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Blackford! on whose uncultured breast,
Among the broom, and thorn, and ''whin'',
A truant-boy, I sought the nest.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, iv. 24.}}}} '''2.''' Same as ''rest-harrow'', 1.—'''Cammock-whin.''' Same as ''cammock''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Cat-whin,''' the dogrose (''Rosa canina''), the<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
